### Position read
The opponent opened R (0,3)->(3,3). We answered B (4,7)->(4,4), so the center is split: opponent at (3,3), us at (4,4). No losses or eliminations. Our Blue center piece has no immediate same-color sandwich threat visible.

### Our plan
Hold (4,4), contest remaining center squares, and look for a same-color setup against R(3,3). On Green’s turn, assess Yellow’s move first; approach the center without blocking Blue mobility or exposing multiple pieces on one capturable line. Stop any three-square center buildup immediately.

### Opponent tendencies
Only evidence is an aggressive first move directly into the center. Expect Yellow to contest (4,3) or pressure Blue vertically.

### Lessons
Moving into a sandwich is safe, but leaving a piece between two opponent pieces of one color is not. Sandwich pairs must match the mover’s color; preserve escape lanes before each opponent cycle.

### Position read
The opponent holds (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; we hold (4,4) with Blue. Green moved (2,0)->(2,4), staging above the only empty center square (3,4). No losses or eliminations. Yellow currently threatens to sandwich B(4,4) by landing a Yellow at (4,5), using Y(4,3) as the far flank, but Blue moves before Yellow.

### Our plan
On Blue’s turn, reassess Red’s move first. Preserve B(4,4) unless Yellow’s (4,5) capture remains available; then move or tactically answer. Contest (3,4), with G(2,4) ready to enter if it remains empty. Seek matching-color flank geometry against the opponent’s adjacent center pieces without friendly fire.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent has committed both opening moves directly to adjacent center squares. Expect Red to take (3,4) or build pressure around B(4,4), while Yellow’s clearest immediate tactic is the horizontal sandwich from (4,5).

### Lessons
Before leaving a center holder in place, scan every same-color enemy landing square on its opposite side. Staged pieces near center should retain open escape lanes and avoid becoming the middle of an immediate sandwich.

### Position read
The opponent holds R(3,3) and Y(4,3); we have G(2,4) above the empty center (3,4). Blue withdrew from (4,4) to (5,4), escaping Yellow’s immediate (4,5) sandwich. No losses. B(5,4) now shares row 5 with B(5,7) and blocks Y(7,4) from advancing directly up column 4.

### Our plan
Keep G(2,4) controlling the column-4 route: it blocks R(1,4) from entering (3,4). Do not put Green on (3,4) while R(3,3) and the open R(0,5)->(3,5) landing still create an immediate sandwich. If Y(4,3) shifts to (4,4), consider contesting without exposing G to Y(7,2)->(4,2). Build same-color Blue geometry from the row-5 pair and protect B(5,4) if Yellow establishes Y(4,4), since Y(7,4)->(6,4) could then capture it next cycle.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is prioritizing central occupation and has already staged R(1,4) behind the center. Expect Yellow to occupy (4,4) or create another center threat.

### Lessons
A center entry is unsound when an enemy same-color flank and reachable landing square bracket it. Preserve blockers that deny those landing routes.

### Position read
We moved G(3,0)->(3,1). The opponent holds R(3,3) and Y(4,3), with Y(4,6) poised for (4,4). G(2,4) still blocks R(1,4) from entering (3,4), but is exposed: R(3,3)->(3,4) would sandwich it against R(1,4), costing us one Green while vacating (3,3). No losses yet.

### Our plan
Keep the center from becoming a four-square occupation. If Red captures G(2,4) and vacates (3,3), G(3,1) can potentially contest that square, but first check the immediate R(0,2)->(3,2) sandwich against R(3,4). If Red retains (3,3) and Yellow takes (4,4), preserve the column-4 blockade and seek a supported challenge. Blue should avoid placing pieces where Y(4,3) and Y(4,6) can create a one-move sandwich.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes central occupation and has established same-color Red geometry that attacks our blocker. Expect either R(3,3)->(3,4) for the capture or continued staging before Y enters (4,4).

### Lessons
A useful blocker may be worth one loss if its capture forces an opponent off a key center square. Recheck the new flanking geometry before occupying any vacated center.

### Position read
We moved B(2,7)->(2,4), creating Blue flanks above R(3,4) and below at B(5,4): B(5,4)->(4,4) will capture that Red if (4,4) stays empty. The opponent currently holds R(3,4) and Y(4,3). Green has 1 loss; all others have 0.

### Our plan
If Yellow does not occupy (4,4), preserve the threatened Blue capture and watch whether Red vacates (3,4). If Yellow plays (4,6)->(4,4), Green must answer G(3,1)->(3,3) to prevent R(3,4)->(3,3) completing the opponent’s center. Expect R(0,2)->(3,2) to capture that Green against R(3,4); afterward Green will be at 2 losses and must be protected. Seek a way to dislodge either R(3,4) or Y(4,4) before committing more pieces.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes center occupation and used the prepared Red flank to capture our blocker. Yellow’s most forcing reply is entry to (4,4); Red may instead be compelled to abandon (3,4) by our new pincer.

### Lessons
Same-color latent flanks can force a center holder to move even when the capture cannot occur immediately. If Yellow blocks the landing square, center defense shifts to Green and its loss count becomes critical.

### Position read
Our Green moved (6,0)->(6,4), safely entering the line Y(4,4)-B(5,4)-G(6,4)-Y(7,4). This blocks Y(7,4)->(6,4), which otherwise captured B(5,4). Losses: our Green 1; all others 0. The opponent occupies (3,4),(4,3),(4,4), but cannot win immediately: R(3,4)->(3,3) vacates (3,4).

### Our plan
On our next Blue turn, if R(3,4), Y(4,4), and B(5,4) remain, move B(2,4) sideways to prepare returning to (2,4), which would capture both center pieces. Keep B(5,4) occupied while G remains at (6,4): vacating it allows Y(4,4)->(5,4) to capture Green against Y(7,4). Reassess if Red vacates (3,4) or attacks the reload square.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes center occupation. Expect Red to disrupt the Blue reload geometry or withdraw R(3,4); Yellow may move Y(4,4) to break the threatened double capture.

### Lessons
Moving into a sandwich is safe. R(3,4)->(3,3) does not complete center because its origin becomes empty; avoid sacrificing Green at (3,3) to a Red sandwich without a genuine immediate threat.

### Position read
Blue moved (5,7)->(5,5), a safe development that opens the right file. Losses remain: our Green 1; others 0. The opponent holds R(3,3), Y(4,3), Y(4,4); center (3,4) is empty. B(2,4) blocks R(1,4)->(3,4), but R(3,3)->(3,4) can capture B(2,4) against R(1,4).

### Our plan
On Green’s turn, first answer any new capture or center threat. If the structure is unchanged, move G(6,4) sideways, preferably toward column 3, freeing B(5,4) to maneuver and removing Green from the Y(4,4)-Y(7,4) sandwich line. Accepting one Blue loss is better than playing B into (3,4), where Yellow and Red have strong multi-capture replies.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is building three-square center control and may use R(3,3)->(3,4) for a capture rather than an immediate center win. Yellow may rearrange the paired center pieces to expose B(5,4) and G(6,4).

### Lessons
Keep B(2,4) in place unless the center is disrupted. Capturing Y(4,4) with B on (3,4) loses material to Y(4,3)->(4,4) and then R landing at (3,5).

### Position read
Green moved (6,4)->(6,3), escaping the latent Y(4,4)-Y(7,4) line that contained B(5,4) and Green. Losses: our Green 1; others 0. The opponent holds R(3,3), Y(4,3), Y(4,4); center (3,4) remains empty. B(2,4) is exposed to R(3,3)->(3,4) against R(1,4), but that move vacates center (3,3).

Expect Red to take B(2,4); do not panic unless it creates an elimination or center tactic. Use Blue to disrupt the opponent’s three-square center structure or build same-color flanks, while keeping B(5,4) out of Yellow’s vertical traps. On Green turns, support the center from (6,3) or create a Green sandwich around exposed center pieces.

The opponent prioritizes compact center control and has built Yellow pairs on row 4. Red has a clean single capture available on B(2,4). Watch for Yellow landing on column 5: with Y(7,5) as a far flank, pieces placed between rows 4-6 may be vulnerable.

### Lessons
Static sandwich geometry captures nothing until an endpoint move triggers it, so escape before the opponent can cycle an endpoint. Preserve Green carefully at two remaining losses.

### Lessons

### Position read
Losses: we have Blue 1, Green 1; opponent 0. The opponent holds R(3,4), Y(4,3), Y(4,4), with Y(3,2) able to enter the empty center (3,3) next turn and complete center occupation. Green cannot reach (3,3): G(3,1) is blocked by Y(3,2), and G(6,3) was blocked by Y(4,3).

G(6,3) moved to (5,3), placing a same-color flank directly below Y(4,3). If play continues, seek a Green landing on (3,3) to capture Y(4,3). Blue should search first for any way to remove a central occupant before Yellow acts.

The opponent prioritizes compact mixed-color center control and uses central pieces to block rook access. Yellow’s move from (4,2) to (3,2) created a direct center-completion threat.

### Lessons
When three enemy team pieces occupy the center, ensure the fourth square is reachable immediately; blockers on both rook approaches can make the threat effectively forced.

### Position read
Losses: we have 1 on each color; the opponent has 0. The opponent occupies three center squares with pieces at (3,4), (4,3), and (4,4). Their piece at (3,2) can legally move to the empty (3,3), completing center occupation immediately. Our acting color had no legal move reaching (3,3) or capturing a current center occupant.

### Our plan
We moved from (5,5) to (4,5). Together with our piece at (5,2), this creates a potential landing at (4,2) that would sandwich and capture both opponent pieces on (4,3)-(4,4) if play continues. Look first for any center-clearing capture or direct center occupation.

The opponent has steadily compacted mixed colors around the center and now has a one-move center win available.

### Lessons
When the opponent controls three center squares, positional counter-threats are insufficient unless the fourth square or an existing occupant can be disrupted before their next move.
